notes:
I've put together notes for every verse, but they're thinner than you hoped in places. I could only read Enduring Word up to about v. 12, and the full Gill page didn't load. For later verses I used short Gill, Pulpit and Barnes extracts from search results. I found no Lutheran or Pentecostal sources, no NET Bible notes, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching, so those are left out. The one place I could clearly show traditions disagreeing is v. 20, with a smaller split at vv. 2 and 18.

**Background: who wrote it and when**
- **Traditional view:** Ellicott says it was written apparently in the year 65-66, while the Apostle was passing through Macedonia, after Paul's first imprisonment in Rome. Guzik agrees: Paul wrote from Macedonia after being released from that imprisonment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/1.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- **Ellicott on the authorship debate:** he says German critics first questioned Paul's authorship in the 1800s. He answers that the unusual vocabulary comes from quoted hymns and sayings, from writing to friends rather than churches, and from Paul's late stage of life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/1.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey notes that Paul's authorship was long assumed, but in the last century and a half or so, that consensus has changed. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/video-gallery/the-pastoral-epistles/ Another Bible Odyssey article calls the Pastoral Letters most likely pseudonymous, meaning written under Paul's name by someone else. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/letters-in-the-ancient-mediterranean-world/
- **An evangelical reply:** a Gospel Coalition article points out an inconsistency. Critics treat differences from Paul's other letters as proof of a forger, but they also treat similarities as evidence of skilful imitation rather than authenticity. https://au.thegospelcoalition.org/article/did-paul-really-write-this-letter/

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Paul stresses his title and his authority so the letter could also serve as Timothy's credentials before the Ephesian church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Guzik: Nero was being called "savior" at the time. Paul makes clear the real Savior is God, in Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Guzik quotes White: the command comes equally from God and from Christ Jesus. White says Paul could hardly write that if he thought Christ was a created being. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Chrysostom (an early Church Father, read in both Orthodox and Catholic tradition): Paul names God as Saviour and Christ as hope to encourage Timothy. Dangers are real, but God is not weak and the hope will not disappoint. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230601.htm

**v. 2**
- **A disagreement over "true child":**
  - Guzik thinks Paul probably led Timothy and his mother to faith on his first missionary journey. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
  - Gill disagrees. He says Timothy was already a believer when Paul met him (Acts 16:1). Paul calls him "son" because of his age or Paul's affection, and "true" sets him apart from nominal Christians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_timothy/1.htm
- Chrysostom: the word "own" shows Timothy's special likeness to Paul as well as Paul's love for him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230601.htm
- On "mercy": Guzik notes that Paul adds it to the greeting only in letters to individuals (Timothy and Titus). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/ Gill takes it as fresh pardon, help in ministry, and support in trials. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_timothy/1.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit Commentary: "urged" is a strong word. It suggests Timothy wanted to go with Paul and had to be persuaded to stay. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_timothy/1.htm
- Guzik: Timothy seems to have wanted to give up and leave. The rest of the chapter gives six reasons to stay. "Charge" is a military word for a strict order. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Chrysostom: Paul doesn't name the false teachers, so that open rebuke wouldn't make them more shameless. He identifies them as Jewish false apostles pushing the Law out of vainglory. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230601.htm
- One older commentator on Bible Hub's page argues that "stay on at Ephesus" shows Timothy was not the established bishop of Ephesus. This bears on later debates about church government. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/1-3.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: the myths were no doubt, purely Rabbinical. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/1.htm
- Another commentary on Bible Hub notes that Ellicott, following Chrysostom, sees Jewish (possibly mystical, "Cabbalistic") roots. In that view the error was only an early stream feeding later Gnosticism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/1-4.htm
- Guzik: these were mostly silly distractions, not a fully formed anti-Christian system. He offers three possibilities: Gnostic-style "emanation" theories, pride in ancestry, or mystical readings of Old Testament genealogies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Chrysostom: God's "stewardship" (he calls it the "dispensation") is received by faith, and endless questioning works against it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230601.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: however firmly Timothy opposes the false teachers, the real aim of all Christian teaching is love. The "commandment" here doesn't mean the Law of Moses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/1.htm
- Ellicott on the order: real, unfeigned faith comes first. Without it there is no good conscience, and without a cleansed conscience no pure heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/1.htm
- Pulpit (StudyLight): the love meant here is love to other people, set against quarrelsome disputes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-timothy-1.html
- Guzik: if time in God's word doesn't produce love, a good conscience and sincere faith, something is wrong. Legalism twists Scripture into harshness and constant guilt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: the Greek pictures missing the target. These teachers had once been on course and were still counted as church members, since Timothy had no authority over outsiders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/1.htm
- Pulpit: the swerve was moral first and then damaged their thinking. How often does the heart determine the bias of the mind! https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-timothy-1.html
- Gill: they left solid gospel doctrine for useless subjects. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_timothy/1.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: they understood neither the fables they taught nor the real truths behind the Law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/1.htm
- Guzik: they didn't grasp what their own teaching implied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/

**vv. 8–9**
- Pulpit: "law" here means the Law of Moses, which these teachers forced on Christians. They didn't realise it was made, not for the righteous, but for sinners. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_timothy/1.htm
- Guzik: the Law exposes sin rather than making anyone righteous. That doesn't mean it says nothing to the righteous, but it speaks especially to the ungodly. Having standards isn't legalism; legalism is thinking your own performance makes you right with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Chrysostom: someone who keeps the law out of love rather than fear is "above" its schooling. A tame horse doesn't need the bit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/1_timothy/1.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: this list follows the Ten Commandments. "Slave traders" (menstealers, kidnappers) were perhaps the worst class of offenders in the Roman world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/1-10.htm
- Pulpit, quoting Ellicott: man-stealing is an extreme breach of the eighth commandment, as the word translated "homosexuals" is of the seventh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/1-10.htm
- "Sound" means "healthy." The word appears only in these letters, in contrast to the sick teaching of the false teachers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/1-10.htm
- Guzik: Ephesus was soaked in these sins, and the false teaching somehow allowed them. That was one more reason for Timothy to stay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/

**v. 11**
- Guzik: the Law can't make anyone righteous, but the gospel can. Paul felt responsible to guard it and pass it on. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- A sermon extract on Bible Hub (author not named) prefers "the gospel of the glory." Paul is describing what the gospel is about, not what kind of thing it is. https://biblehub.com/study/1_timothy/1-20.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: Paul was "counted faithful." Faithfulness doesn't need talent, and believers are servants under duty, not volunteers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Chrysostom quotes vv. 12–13 as an example of Paul's humility. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220138.htm

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: Paul was a blasphemer because he spoke against the name of Jesus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_timothy/1.htm
- Gill, a Baptist with a strong view of God's sovereignty: Paul's ignorance wasn't the reason he received mercy, since mercy is always given freely. It only shows that what he received really was mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_timothy/1.htm
- Guzik: Paul's past didn't disqualify him, and he was encouraging a Timothy who probably felt unworthy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/

**v. 14**
- Chrysostom: grace didn't just abound but "abounded exceedingly." Faith alone isn't enough; love is needed too, because many who believe Christ is God don't love him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/1_timothy/1.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik: calling himself the worst of sinners wasn't false humility. Paul had forced Christians under torture to blaspheme Christ, and he felt especially guilty for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Ellicott thinks "trustworthy saying" introduces well-known Christian watchwords. There are five such sayings in the Pastoral letters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/1.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: Paul is a "pattern," so no sinner can say they are too far gone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Gill: God's purpose in Paul's conversion was to encourage others to believe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_timothy/1.htm
- Pulpit: the phrase "believe in Him" here carries the sense of resting or leaning on him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_timothy/1.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: this prayer of praise differs a little from Paul's usual ones and should read "the only God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_timothy/1.htm
- Guzik: the outburst shows Paul both knew God and loved him, and trouble worshipping comes from not knowing God well. This great God was another reason for Timothy to stay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/

**v. 18 (the prophecies about Timothy: readings differ)**
- Pulpit: Paul gave the charge as the Holy Spirit directed, through the church's prophets, who had pointed out Timothy for this battle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_timothy/1.htm
- Gill: these were not Old Testament prophecies or private revelations to Paul. More likely they were the good reports about Timothy from believers at Lystra and Iconium. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_timothy/1.htm
- Guzik (a Calvary Chapel pastor): the prophecies were meant to strengthen Timothy, but Paul keeps his eyes on the present fight, not on predictions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-1/
- Pulpit: the fight is good because it is against evil, for people's good, and for God's glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-timothy-1.html

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: as in v. 5, Paul pairs faith with a clean conscience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/1-19.htm
- An older commentator on Bible Hub: men's holiness is proportioned to their soundness in the faith. Love of some sin usually leads people into false belief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/1-19.htm

**v. 20 (handed over to Satan: the traditions really differ)**
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** this was excommunication along with bodily disease or death, a power apparently held only by apostles. https://biblehub.com/1_timothy/1-20.htm
- **Baptist (Gill):** this was not excommunication, which is the whole church's act. It was Paul's personal apostolic power to hand bodies over to Satan to be afflicted, so the men would recognise their sin. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/1-timothy/1-20.html
- **Baptist (MacArthur, gty.org):** the verb means to abandon, taking away God's protection. He sees this as part of the church's ministry and something Timothy was invited to do too. https://www.gty.org/sermons/54-9/delivered-to-satan-part-1
- **Reformed (Calvin):** outside the church there is only Satan's rule. Someone cast out is under Satan for a time, until reconciled. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/1-20.html
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** shorthand for church discipline. Paul apparently didn't think the two had committed the unpardonable sin. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/disciplining-blasphemers
- **An older commentator on Bible Hub:** some see Satan torturing the excommunicated, but we find nothing of this in Scripture. It simply means being put out into the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/1-20.htm
- **Methodist (Wesley):** the aim was that suffering would restrain them even if they didn't repent. **Clarke:** nobody alive knows exactly what this punishment was. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/1-20.html
- **Catholic (Haydock):** it means excommunication. Citing Chrysostom, he adds that the devil often afflicted the excommunicated with illness at that time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/1-20.html
- **Shared ground:** the purpose was correction, not damnation. Hymenaeus probably reappears in 2 Tim 2:17–18, and Alexander may be the man in 2 Tim 4:14. https://biblehub.com/study/1_timothy/1-20.htm
